{{Short description|Field arising from a quotient ring by a maximal ideal}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''residue field''' is a basic construction in [[commutative algebra]]. If <math>R</math> is a [[commutative ring]] and <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is a [[maximal ideal]], then the residue field is the [[quotient ring]] <math>k=R/\mathfrak{m}</math>, which is a [[field (mathematics)|field]].<ref>{{cite book
| last1 = Dummit
| first1 = D. S.
| last2 = Foote
| first2 = R.
| title = Abstract Algebra
| publisher = Wiley
| year = 2004
| edition = 3
| isbn = 9780471433347 
}}</ref> Frequently, <math>R</math> is a [[local ring]] and <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is then its unique maximal ideal.

In abstract algebra, the [[splitting field]] of a polynomial is constructed using residue fields. Residue fields also applied in [[algebraic geometry]], where to every point <math>x</math> of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] <math>X</math> one associates its residue field <math>k(x)</math>.<ref>{{cite book
 | author = David Mumford
 | author-link = David Mumford
 | year = 1999
 | title = The Red Book of Varieties and Schemes: Includes the Michigan Lectures (1974) on Curves and Their Jacobians
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | volume = 1358
 | edition = 2nd
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | doi = 10.1007/b62130
 | isbn = 3-540-63293-X
}}</ref>  One can say a little loosely that the residue field of a point of an abstract [[algebraic variety]] is the ''natural domain'' for the coordinates of the point.{{clarify|date=February 2015}}<!-- what is a "natural domain"? -->

==Definition==
Suppose that <math>R</math> is a commutative [[local ring]], with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>. Then the '''residue field''' is the quotient ring <math>R/\mathfrak{m}</math>.

Now suppose that <math>X</math> is a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] and <math>x</math> is a point of <math>X</math>. By the definition of a scheme, we may find an affine [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighbourhood]] <math>\mathcal{U} = \text{Spec}(A)</math> of <math>x</math>, with some [[commutative ring]] <math>A</math>. Considered in the neighbourhood <math>\mathcal{U}</math>, the point <math>x</math> corresponds to a [[prime ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{p} \subseteq A</math> (see [[Zariski topology]]). The ''[[local ring]]'' of <math>X</math>  at <math>x</math> is by definition the [[localization of a ring|localization]] <math>A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math>  of <math>A</math> by <math>A\setminus \mathfrak{p}</math>, and <math>A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> has maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}=\mathfrak{p}  A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math>. Applying the construction above, we obtain the '''residue field of the point <math>x</math>''':

:<math>k(x) := A_{\mathfrak{p}}/\mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}} </math>.

Since localization is [[exact functor|exact]], <math>k(x)</math> is the [[field of fractions]] of <math>A/\mathfrak p</math> (which is an [[integral domain]] as <math>\mathfrak p</math> is a prime ideal).<ref>{{Matsumura CA}}, 1.K</ref> One can prove that this definition does not depend on the choice of the affine neighbourhood <math>\mathcal{U}</math>.<ref>Intuitively, the residue field of a point is a local invariant. Axioms of schemes are set up in such a way as to assure the compatibility between various affine open neighborhoods of a point, which implies the statement.</ref>

A point is called [[rational point|<math>\color{blue}k</math>-rational]] for a certain field <math>k</math>, if <math>k(x)=k</math>.<ref>[[Ulrich Görtz|Görtz, Ulrich]] and Wedhorn, Torsten. ''Algebraic Geometry: Part 1: Schemes'' (2010)  Vieweg+Teubner Verlag.</ref>

==Example==
Consider the [[affine line]] <math>\mathbb{A}^1(k)=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t])</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math>. If <math>k</math>  is [[algebraically closed field|algebraically closed]], there are exactly two types of prime ideals, namely

*<math>(t-a),\,a \in k</math>  
*<math>(0)</math>, the zero-ideal.

The residue fields are

*<math>k[t]_{(t-a)}/(t-a)k[t]_{(t-a)} \cong k</math>
*<math>k[t]_{(0)} \cong k(t)</math>, the function field over ''k'' in one variable.

If <math>k</math> is not algebraically closed, then more types arise from the [[irreducible polynomial]]s of degree greater than 1. For example if <math>k=\mathbb{R}</math>, then the prime ideals generated by quadratic irreducible polynomials (such as <math>x^2+1</math>) all have residue field isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{C}</math>.

==Properties==
* For a scheme locally of [[morphism of finite type|finite type]] over a field <math>k</math>, a point <math>x</math> is [[closed point|closed]] if and only if <math>k(x)</math> is a finite extension of the base field <math>k</math>. This is a geometric formulation of [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]]. In the above example, the points of the first kind are closed, having residue field <math>k</math>, whereas the second point is the [[generic point]], having [[transcendence degree]] 1 over <math>k</math>. 
* A [[morphism of schemes|morphism]] <math>\operatorname{Spec}(K) \rightarrow X</math>, <math>K</math> some field, is equivalent to giving a point <math>x \in X</math> and an [[field extension|extension]] <math>K/k(x)</math>.
* The [[Dimension of a scheme|dimension]] of a scheme of finite type over a field is equal to the transcendence degree of the residue field of the generic point.
